items.title: Trump unveils new tariffs to fight excess factory capacity, undeterred by midterms defeat
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Nov 25 (Reuters) - US President Donald Trump on Wednesday fired a new tariff salvo on 14 major trading partners including China, Japan and the European Union, undeterred in his protectionist push by the losses his Republican Party suffered in US midterm elections.

His administration proposed new headline tariff rates of 20% to 40%, but said duties would be capped at lower levels agreed under trade deals that have already been concluded or remain under negotiation.

Separately, the United States Trade Representative proposed a new 10% tariff on imports of Brazil's finished Embraer commercial aircraft, and to raise duties on imports of Brazilian sugar that exceed quotas as part of an effort to push Brasilia to rectify alleged unfair trade practices.

The products were previously exempted from Trump's 25% tariffs on Brazilian goods that were imposed in July. A US official said that despite negotiations, there were "substantial differences" over the allegations.

Under the main "Section 301" probe into excess industrial capacity, China would face the highest capped rate of 20%, which would be added to duties of roughly 25% imposed during Trump's first term.

That rate would comply with a US-China trade truce that expires on January 10. But if the truce unravels, China's rate would rise to 40%, the USTR said.

Vietnam would face a capped tariff rate of 20% if it reaches a trade agreement with Washington, rising to 35% if negotiations fail.

US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said the tariffs, which would not take effect until after a January 25 public hearing, were intended to counteract "industrial strategies built on targeting manufacturing, wage and labor suppression, financial and other support, non-market economy inputs, and other market-distorting practices" that undermine the US manufacturing base.

Washington has long accused China of subsidizing industry and flooding global markets with low-cost exports ranging from steel to electric vehicles and solar products.

Beijing earlier reiterated its opposition to "trade wars" and rejected allegations of overcapacity, but stopped short of threatening retaliation.

'FALSE ISSUE,' CHINA SAYS

"The so-called 'overcapacity' is a false issue, and China opposes using it as an excuse for political manipulation," Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun said, urging the world's top two economies to maintain stable relations.

The USTR also proposed capped tariff rates of 18% for imported goods from Cambodia, Indonesia, Malaysia, Thailand and Bangladesh, and 15%, including existing "Most Favored Nation" duties, for Japan, South Korea, Taiwan, the EU and Switzerland.

India, which has yet to reach a trade deal with the Trump administration, would face a 17% tariff rate if an agreement is finalized and a 25% rate if talks fail, the USTR said. Singapore would receive a capped tariff rate of 10%.

Greer told CNBC the proposed caps were consistent with trade agreements reached over the past year that also lowered barriers to US exports.

"We're sticking to that in terms of our proposals because we think a lot of these deals we made actually solve a lot of the problems we see in excess capacity or can go toward it," Greer said. "So you know we've talked to our trading partners about this. They know what we're proposing. I think a lot of this is baked in."

Mexico and Norway were excluded from the proposals because investigations into their trade practices remain under way, Greer said.

Even so, the prospect of new trade barriers weighed on stock markets on Wednesday amid a renewed selloff in tech stocks. Major US indexes opened down more than 1%, with the tech-heavy Nasdaq composite (.IXIC) down more than 3%.

"It is another reminder that while the legal justification for tariffs keeps changing, US protectionism is becoming increasingly difficult to unwind," ING analysts wrote.

NEW DUTIES WON'T EXCEED NEGOTIATED LIMITS

Trump's tariffs have contributed to higher prices for US consumers, and a Reuters/Ipsos opinion poll conducted after Republicans' midterm losses found 62% of respondents supported efforts to repeal them.

But Trump has long vowed to restore duties struck down by the US Supreme Court in February. The latest measures follow an eight-month investigation into unfair trade practices under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974.

Greer said the proposed tariffs would not apply to about $30 billion of Chinese imports under consideration for tariff reductions through a bilateral mechanism known as the Board of Trade.

However, the new duties would be added to tariffs imposed on Chinese goods during Trump's first term, which total roughly 25%.

They would not be imposed on top of the 10% and 12.5% tariffs introduced in July on a broader group of 60 trading partners over allegations of lax enforcement of anti-forced-labor laws.

Reporting by David Lawder and Andrea Shalal, additional reporting by Jasper Ward; Editing by Tomasz Janowski and Mark Potter

items.title: 'I'm going to drive': FAA outage and high fares reshape Thanksgiving travel plans
items.content_html:
NEW YORK, Nov 25 (Reuters) - Dinese Jackson couldn't stomach spending roughly $1,500 to fly herself and her two children from Raleigh, North Carolina, to Dallas, Texas, for Thanksgiving, more than double what she had paid for similar trips in the past.

Still, she kept checking airfares in hopes fares would drop, until the Federal Aviation Administration's nationwide ground stop on November 13 cemented her decision to make the trip by car instead, even at the price of a 17-hour drive.

"When that happened on Friday, I was like, 'Yep, I'm keeping my car reservation. I'm going to go ahead and drive for sure," the 51-year-old credit analyst told Reuters. "For those that are flying, I just think it's going to be chaos."

A router outage on November 13 caused a communications failure at air traffic control centers and triggered a nearly five-hour nationwide disruption impacting more than 18,000 flights and affecting about 1 million passengers.

Just a few days later, travelers faced fresh disruptions when United Airlines (UAL.O) suffered a widespread technology outage and Delta Air Lines' (DAL.N) automated weight-and-balance system failed on Sunday, delaying more than 2,000 flights nationwide, shaking confidence in air travel ahead of the Thanksgiving travel rush.

The rising cost of airfare, which has hit 10-year highs for the holiday period, had already persuaded some Americans to stay home this year. Airlines for America forecast nearly 29 million passengers will travel between November 20 and 30, down from last year's forecast of 31 million passengers.

HIGHEST AIRFARE IN A DECADE

Two weeks before Thanksgiving, domestic airfares for the holiday travel period averaged about $469 in 2026, about a 57% year-over-year increase, according to data from travel search engine, Kayak. Travel booking app Hopper said months of elevated jet fuel costs due to the conflict in Iran have helped push Thanksgiving and Christmas fares to 10-year highs.

United Airlines (UAL.O) said it expects more than 6.6 million customers over a 12-day period, on par with last year. American Airlines (AAL.O) said it plans to welcome 8 million travelers in the same period, and plans to operate 4% more flights than in 2025. US airlines are operating 2% more flights on average this Thanksgiving than last year, while seat capacity is up 1%, Cirium, a flight analytics company, said.

Fewer Americans are traveling by air in 2026 as fares rise and disruptions mount. The last time the Transportation Security Administration screened more than 3 million passengers in a single day was November 30, 2025. The TSA has not screened 3 million passengers on any day this year, compared to eight times in 2025.

During the Thanksgiving Holiday, the agency expects to screen about 3% fewer passengers year-on-year.

Jennifer Shaw, 57, was less than thrilled to learn her son planned to forfeit his non-refundable plane ticket home from college in Michigan. Instead, he opted to drive 10 hours to Monmouth County, New Jersey, with friends rather than risk getting stranded at an airport during the holiday rush.

"Even though I might be worried that he's driving 10 hours with a group of boys, at least I don't have to worry about the airlines," Shaw said.

The FAA warned stormy weather could affect flights throughout the week.

A PAUSE IN UPGRADES

FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford said last week the agency was "very close" to being able to disclose the root cause of the router outage. The FAA declined to say Monday when it plans to offer an update.

On November 17, the FAA said it had immediately paused deployment of additional routers.

"I'm hoping the government is not going to do any more upgrades during this time that we're going to be away," said retiree Liz Dougherty, 63, who plans to fly from North Carolina to Spain to take a cruise for the holiday, adding that the November 13 flight halt was "definitely in the back of my mind."

About 81.5 million Americans will travel at least 50 miles for Thanksgiving over a six-day period, according to AAA estimates, down only slightly from last year's total of 81.6 million. However, more Americans are expected to take cruises, buses, and trains to their destinations.

Bus and travel search engine, Wanderu, said the ground stop gave the company its busiest day of the year so far, with bookings made that Friday up about 16% from last year. Bus operator Flix North America said bookings for Thanksgiving are up 17% from last year.

Amtrak said the company is again expecting a record in 2026 after 1.2 million customer trips during last year's Thanksgiving holiday.

items.title: US House Democrats expand probe into Trump Jr.'s investments
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Nov 24 (Reuters) - US House Democrats probing Donald Trump Jr.'s business dealings have sought records from prediction market firm Polymarket, vaping company Juul and two other companies tied to 1789 Capital, the venture capital firm where the president's son is a partner.

In letters published on Tuesday, US Representative Jamie Raskin, a Maryland Democrat expected to chair the House Judiciary Committee next year, asked the companies — which also include GrabAGun (PEW.N) and Hadrian Automation — for a range of records of communications with 1789 Capital and its executives.

"The probe examines whether the President's son and his business partners helped steer federal contracts or regulatory decisions to companies in which they had a significant financial interest or used advance knowledge of those forthcoming decisions to make investments and profit," Raskin's office wrote in a press release. Raskin opened the probe in August.

Democrats, who take control of Congress in January, are preparing a flurry of investigations into Republican President Donald Trump and his administration, from contracts and potential conflicts of interest, to immigration and the investigation into the late financier and convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.

1789 Capital President Omeed Malik and Trump Jr. denied any wrongdoing at an Axios event last week.

"We responded to Congressman Raskin back in September pointing out in detail the many flaws in his understanding of how 1789 has operated and a number of basic factual errors," Bill Burck, an attorney representing 1789 Capital, said in a statement. "These are personal attacks untethered to actual evidence."

Juul said it intended "to cooperate with any Congressional effort to understand our company."

A representative for online gun retailer GrabAGun said: "Congressman Raskin's letter is a political document, and its allegations are baseless."

Representatives for Trump Jr., Polymarket and Hadrian Automation did not immediately return requests for comment.

In a move legal experts say will likely face challenges, President Donald Trump sought on Friday to curb cooperation between the private sector and Congress, ordering companies with federal contracts to alert the White House before sharing information with lawmakers, and to withhold material deemed confidential.

Under the US Constitution, Congress has oversight powers and authority to obtain information, including via subpoenas that the administration has sought to limit in scope.

RASKIN HIGHLIGHTS TIMING OF INVESTMENTS

Raskin's expanded investigation focuses on how the four companies "benefited, or stand to benefit," from Trump administration contracts, regulatory decisions or proposed rule changes, which Raskin said could point to conflicts of interest or other misconduct.

In his letter to Polymarket, Raskin said that the company had effectively been banned from the US and was also under federal investigation before Trump returned to office.

In July 2025, regulators closed that probe and approved Polymarket's acquisition of a US platform that paved the way for it to re-enter the US market. The following month, Polymarket disclosed that 1789 Capital had made a strategic investment, Raskin wrote. Reuters and other outlets reported at the time that the investment was worth tens of millions of dollars.

Reuters reported last month that the Commodity Futures Trading Commission has reopened its probe into Polymarket.

Raskin also said that in July 2025, months after 1789 Capital made a $5 million investment in Juul, authorities eased restrictions on sales of some Juul products, with more authorized earlier this year.

GrabAGun went public in 2025 after merging with a special-purpose acquisition company backed by Malik. In May 2026, the Trump administration proposed rules to make it easier to direct-ship guns to customers, Raskin also said.

The GrabAGun representative said the proposed rule changes were well known across the industry and that the company only provided input through the public comment process.

Raskin also wrote to Hadrian Automation, saying that the manufacturing company won US government contracts worth nearly $1 billion shortly after 1789 Capital acquired a stake in the company.

Raskin said that the president himself has publicly acknowledged the business conflicts, telling CNBC in July: "I feel badly in a way for my kids ... Almost anything they do ... they have inside information."

items.title: US Army conducts controlled detonation of lead-based explosives stockpile in Iowa
items.content_html:
MIDDLETOWN, Iowa, Nov 25 (Reuters) - The US government on Wednesday conducted its planned detonation of an aging stockpile of lead-based explosives at a US Army munitions depot, as residents of an adjacent tiny Iowa farm town hunkered down in their homes to avoid any toxic dust emitted from the blast.

The Environmental Protection Agency said its teams of emission monitors reported detecting zero levels of airborne lead in the surrounding region immediately after the explosion.

The detonation followed days of public rancor and legal wrangling over the controversial disposal plan, which authorities said was far safer than waiting for the deteriorating chemical drums to eventually blow up on their own.

Shortly after 9 a.m. CST (1500 GMT), the Federal Emergency Management Agency posted a message on its X account confirming the detonation had been carried out and urging nearby residents to remain indoors for the time being.

"Following this morning's controlled detonation in Middletown, Iowa, residents within 20 miles who have not evacuated should continue to shelter in place and follow @EPA safety guidance until given the all clear by officials. FEMA has provided safe lodging to those who evacuated," the agency wrote.

A short time later, Army Secretary Aaron Telle declared that the "controlled, mitigated detonation," designed to dispose of nearly 5 tons (4,500 kg) of highly unstable lead azide stored in 68 degrading plastic barrels, had "exceeded all expectations and was a huge success."

"The threat of a spontaneous detonation has been eliminated," he said on X.

One hour after the blast, EPA chief Lee Zeldin told CNN, "Real-time air monitors are reporting zero detection of airborne lead throughout the region," EPA said in a separate statement. "As far as the blast itself, it caved inward perfectly."

In a live television feed from the site at the scheduled detonation time, the sound of an apparent explosion could be heard and a wisp of what appeared to be gray smoke was seen rising into the dawn-lit sky from beyond a line of trees before quickly dissipating.

Public safety concerns had focused on expectations that the explosion would spew a plume of toxic lead dust over homes, crops and livestock beyond the detonation site at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown, about 150 miles southwest of the state capital Des Moines.

On Tuesday, federal, state and local officials alerted residents to evacuation plans and bolstered an array of measures designed to curb the fallout, while assuring the public that the operation was under control.

The EPA said it had collected more than 1,200 air, soil and water samples for comparison to further sampling to be done on Wednesday after the explosion.

'CONTROLLED, MITIGATED DETONATION'

Experts from the Army, EPA, the US Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives and others stressed their consensus that the controlled detonation of the lead azide stockpile was the safest option for disposing of it.

Otherwise, they said, the increasingly volatile material, growing more unstable with the arrival of colder weather, was certain to eventually explode on its own. Experts likewise concluded that any attempt to chemically neutralize or relocate the storage drums would likely trigger an uncontrolled blast.

Army projections released on Tuesday had shown that lead dust could settle on surfaces as far as 40 miles southwest of the blast site, extending through southeastern Iowa into northern Missouri. Airborne particles could travel nearly 100 miles within eight hours, according to projections.

Some residents said changing guidance over the timing of the blast and the likely path of the lead plume had left them confused and frustrated.

Farmers and ranchers worried about protecting their crops and herds. US and Iowa agriculture officials estimated that 350 farms could be impacted by lead fallout, based on the anticipated direction of the plume.

At Tuesday's press conference, officials said they had constructed a range of containment structures and equipment they hoped would minimize the lead particulates belched from the detonation. Those measures included earthen berms along with two towering walls stacked with tanks of water for release into the blast zone.

Engineers also installed a misting apparatus to dampen the surrounding terrain and a system to flood the blast site with aqueous foam to capture dust.

In the hours following Wednesday's blast, it was not yet clear how well those measures worked.

Lead azide has long been used as the chief detonating material in military ordnance. The explosive chemical was deemed largely obsolete years ago, and the Army brought unused stockpiles from bases around the country to Iowa in 2009.

During an inspection in March, officials discovered a dangerous crystallization of the storage drums and material in them, a sign that it had become dangerously unstable, spurring deliberations over the safest way to dispose of it.

items.title: US third-quarter economic growth revised sharply higher; inflation broadening out
items.content_html:
Summary:

  • Gross domestic product growth revised to 4.3% pace in third quarter from previous 3.4% rate
  • Consumer spending, business investment account for upgrade to GDP growth
  • Personal Consumption Expenditures Price Index increases 0.3% in October; up 3.8% year-over-year
  • Core PCE inflation rises 0.3% for third straight month; advances 3.3% year-over-year

WASHINGTON, Nov 25 (Reuters) - The US economy grew much faster than initially estimated in the third quarter, while inflation increased further in October, reinforcing expectations that the Federal Reserve will raise interest rates next month and again in early 2027.

The sharp upward revision to gross domestic product last quarter, reported by the Commerce Department on Wednesday, marked the quickest economic growth pace in three years. It reflected upgrades to consumer spending and business investment, mostly related to artificial intelligence.

Robust domestic demand is fueling inflation, with a measure of underlying price pressures in October posting its biggest year-on-year increase since late 2023. The economy has powered ahead despite the ongoing US-Israeli war with Iran.

"It is more urgent than ever that Fed officials step up the pace of interest rate hikes to cool off economic demand," said Christopher Rupkey, chief economist at FWDBONDS. "It was once thought that import tariffs and energy prices from the Mideast war were one-off factors behind the higher inflation numbers, but increasingly the inflation fires look to be stoked by old-fashioned economic demand pressures."

GDP increased at a 4.3% annualized rate last quarter, the Commerce Department's Bureau of Economic Analysis said in its second estimate of third-quarter GDP. It was the fastest pace since the third quarter of 2023. The economy was previously estimated to have grown at a 3.4% pace.

Economists polled by Reuters had expected GDP growth would be revised up to a 3.5% pace. The economy grew at a 2.2% rate in the April-June quarter. Growth in consumer spending, which accounts for more than two-thirds of the economy, was revised up to a 4.2% rate from the previously reported 3.8% pace.

Spending is being driven mostly by higher-income households, whose wealth was boosted by the stock market before the ongoing AI-led selloff. Historically low layoffs and moderate hiring are also helping other households to sustain spending, though wage gains have at times lagged inflation. Households are also saving less and dipping into their nest eggs.

Business spending on equipment increased at a 21.8% rate. That was an upgrade from the 20.9% rate of growth estimated last month. Business investment has posted three straight quarters of double-digit growth, and momentum appeared to have persisted early in the fourth quarter.

A separate report from the Commerce Department's Census Bureau showed non-defense capital goods orders excluding aircraft, a proxy for business spending, jumped 1.2% in October after rising 0.8% in September. Shipments of these so-called core capital goods, which go into the calculation of the business spending on equipment component in the GDP report, rose 0.6% last month after advancing 1.3% in September.

GROWING QUESTIONS OVER AI FUNDING

A cloud is hanging over AI. Broader questions about AI funding, profitability, regulation and public resistance to data center developments have arisen and remain even after the surprise reinstatement of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang. Tech firms have borrowed huge sums over the past year for AI spending.

AI remains a key pillar of the economy.

Final sales to private domestic purchasers, which exclude inventories, trade and government, accelerated at a 5.8% rate, the fastest pace since the second quarter of 2021, the GDP report showed. This measure of domestic demand, closely watched by policymakers, was previously estimated to have surged at a 4.9% rate.

The Personal Consumption Expenditures Price Index increased 0.3% in October after gaining 0.5% in September, the BEA said in a separate report. In the 12 months through October, PCE inflation increased 3.8% after advancing 3.6% in September. The rise in PCE inflation was in line with economists' expectations.

Excluding the volatile food and energy components, the PCE Price Index increased 0.3% for the third straight month. The so-called core PCE inflation increased 3.3% on a year-over-year basis in October, the largest advance since November 2023, after climbing 3.1% in September.

The US Fed tracks the PCE price measures for its 2% inflation target. Financial markets have priced in a quarter-percentage-point rate hike at the US central bank's December 8-9 meeting from the current 3.75%-4.00% range, and expected another increase in January, CME Group's FedWatch tool showed.

Fed Governor Christopher Waller has signaled he could support a bigger half-percentage-point increase to quell inflation.

Stocks on Wall Street were trading lower. The dollar rose against a basket of currencies. US Treasury yields fell.

The economy's resilience was reinforced by a report from the Labor Department showing initial claims for state unemployment benefits dropped 13,000 to a seasonally adjusted 189,000 for the week ended November 21. Claims have been running at very low levels since mid-July.

The number of people receiving unemployment benefits after an initial week of aid, a proxy for hiring, tumbled 95,000 to a seasonally adjusted 1.697 million during the week ended November 14, the claims report showed. The so-called continuing claims covered the period during which the government surveyed households for November's unemployment rate.

The jobless rate dropped from 4.5% in November last year to 4.1% in October, though part of the decrease has been due to a smaller labor force due to retirements and the Trump administration's immigration crackdown.

Reporting by Lucia Mutikani; Editing by Chizu Nomiyama and Paul Simao

items.title: US grocers serve up Thanksgiving deals even as turkey prices climb
items.content_html:
NEW YORK/CHICAGO, Nov 25 (Reuters) - Major US retailers including Walmart (WMT.O) are offering Thanksgiving meal kits at or below last year's prices to woo shoppers weary of inflation. But the grocers face an inconvenient truth: wholesale prices for turkey and potatoes, the holiday's two marquee staples, have jumped since last year, forcing them to eat some extra costs.

Their hope is that, once inside, shoppers are indulging in drinks, snacks and desserts, industry analysts say.

"Turkey and other highly visible Thanksgiving staples are important price signals for shoppers," said Sally Lyons Wyatt, consumer packaged goods lead at research firm Circana. "Retailers have an incentive to promote aggressively or absorb some cost pressure to reinforce the value of the overall meal."

This month, when voters roundly punished US President Donald Trump's Republican Party in the US midterm elections, affordability emerged as a top concern, exit polls showed.

Wholesale price assessments for frozen tom turkeys were up 12% from a year earlier at a record high of $2 per pound as of November 9, according to commodity data firm Expana.

Yet retailers are holding the line: in the four weeks to November 7, whole-bird turkeys from the frozen section were 6.3% less per pound than in the same period last year, data from NielsenIQ showed. For russet potatoes, wholesale prices soared about 46%, Expana found — yet in retail stores, a 3-pound bag cost just 2.9% more year-over-year, the NielsenIQ data revealed.

Last year, as tariffs roiled global markets, Trump pointed to Walmart's generously discounted $40 Thanksgiving deal as evidence that prices were under control.

This year, with inflation and gas prices shrinking shoppers' wallets, Walmart is going even lower. The US giant unveiled a 26-item, $35 Thanksgiving meal kit that can feed 10 people, with turkeys ranging from 10 to 16 pounds. It's $5 cheaper than last year's, with four extra items.

Not to be outdone, German discount grocer Lidl announced a 10-person Thanksgiving package featuring 29 items and a 14-pound turkey, for $33.56. Lidl, which had initially set the price $2 higher, moved it gradually lower in November, promising on its website it "will not be beaten ... by Walmart."

Michael Swanson, chief agricultural economist at Wells Fargo, called these approaches loss-leading strategies, aimed at using discounts on popular items to lure shoppers. Once in the store, "you also load up on chocolates and sweets ... and suddenly you'll be spending quite a bit of money," Swanson said.

MANAGING COSTS

Even though aggressive meal deals can eat into profit margins, grocers can offset at least a portion of added costs by including products in kits that have become cheaper at wholesale, said Alexis Villacis, an agricultural economist at Ohio State University.

For example, wholesale ham prices had fallen 32% year over year as of October, Expana found. But according to NielsenIQ, families that eschew turkey for a whole ham on Thanksgiving were paying only 15.5% less per pound in the four weeks ended November 7.

Major retailers can also protect margins by negotiating favorable deals with suppliers. "Retailers like Kroger (KR.N) and Walmart, they have the upper hand," Villacis said. "If they want to push the turkey industry to give them discounts, they have the power to do so."

However, both suppliers and grocers were bound to absorb some incremental costs for rising input costs, such as diesel fuel: "If consumers pay similar prices as last year, and you have input costs that are higher, the costs have to be absorbed somewhere," said Scott Vinson, an executive vice president of turkey company Butterball.

DEVIL IS IN THE DETAILS

At low-priced German-owned chain Aldi, a $39, 10-person dinner is a tick more affordable than last year's $40 deal but includes just 15 items versus 26 last year. It does not include russet potatoes.

Aldi Chief Commercial Officer Scott Patton attributed the smaller basket to Aldi's decision to build the meal around an annual American Farm Bureau Federation benchmark tracking the cost of a classic Thanksgiving meal. Comparing this year to last, Patton said, "isn't apples-to-apples and doesn't reflect the value we're delivering."

The Farm Bureau pegged the average cost of Thanksgiving dinner for 10 people at $58.63, up 6% from last year. It said the cost of a 16-pound turkey jumped about 10% to $1.48 per pound, but shoppers found deals for as low as 69 cents per pound.

Wells Fargo forecast the average 10-person Thanksgiving meal to cost $79 this year. That is more than double what the value retailers are charging, yet still less than $8 per person — quite modest for a multi-course culinary bonanza, Swanson said.

If the race to cut prices leads to a drop in quality, it could backfire: "People are open to trade-offs," Swanson said. "They're not open to rip-offs."

Reporting by Nicholas P. Brown in New York and Tom Polansek in Chicago. Editing by Lisa Jucca and Nick Zieminski

items.title: Salvadoran migrant Kilmar Abrego Garcia lands in Spain after US departure deal
items.content_html:
MADRID, Nov 25 (Reuters) - Salvadoran migrant Kilmar Abrego Garcia, whose wrongful deportation to El Salvador made him a focus for critics of President Donald Trump's immigration crackdown, arrived in Spain on Wednesday after leaving the US under a deal with the authorities.

Reuters witnesses saw Abrego Garcia, 31, who was wearing a Chicago Bulls cap and sunglasses, leave the airport building and board a car, without making any comment.

Abrego Garcia's arrival in Spain brings to a close a legal battle that reached the US Supreme Court after authorities deported him to a megaprison in El Salvador in March 2025 despite a court order barring his return there because of the risk of persecution.

His lawyer, Simon Sandoval-Moshenberg, told reporters in Madrid his client's departure from the US, as a free man to the country of his choice on a commercial flight, was a victory because it was what he had been seeking since August 2025.

LAWYER SAYS MOVE TO SPAIN IS TEMPORARY

The lawyer has said the move to Spain is temporary and that Abrego Garcia could have legal avenues to return to the US under a future administration.

"We understand that under the Trump administration, he's never going to get a fair shake," the lawyer said.

"Kilmar Abrego Garcia is going to last a lot longer than Donald Trump, and he will be back in the United States as a lawful permanent resident under the next administration."

Spain has been a target of criticism by the Trump administration over the Socialist-led government's decision to regularise hundreds of thousands of illegal migrants. The criticism intensified after a mass crossing by over 80,000 migrants to its North African enclave of Ceuta in late July.

The US Department of Homeland Security said in a post on X Abrego Garcia had "self-deported" to Spain, adding that it was unsurprised by his choice of "a country that earlier this year was invaded by tens of thousands of illegal aliens".

"Spain's radical open-border policies have made the once-great country a breeding ground for illegal migrants," it said.

US officials had called Abrego Garcia's removal to El Salvador an "administrative error", but for months said they could not bring him back.

Ordered by the US Supreme Court to facilitate Abrego Garcia's return, the Trump administration ultimately brought him back to the US in June 2025. It later attempted to deport him to Liberia on a human smuggling charge that was dismissed by a US judge.

items.title: US finds no evidence China directed executive to spy on Nvidia CEO, WSJ reports
items.content_html:
Nov 25 (Reuters) - US officials found no evidence that tech executive Alice Huang was directed by Beijing to spy on Nvidia (NVDA.O) CEO Jensen Huang, the Wall Street Journal reported on Wednesday, citing people familiar with a classified briefing.

The briefing comes after US President Donald Trump cleared the way for Jensen Huang's reinstatement earlier this week, assuring Nvidia that its CEO posed no national-security threat.

The controversy began with concerns over Alice Huang's alleged Chinese intelligence links and whether her relationship with Jensen Huang affected suspected diversions of Nvidia chips to China.

Officials from the CIA, FBI, Office of the Director of National Intelligence and National Security Agency briefed staff from congressional intelligence committees and chamber leaders, the Journal reported.

The officials said Alice Huang contacted China's spy agency during the affair but found no indication that she provided significant intelligence, the Journal reported.

Nvidia and the agencies did not immediately respond to a Reuters request for comment. Reuters could not independently verify the report.

Shares of Nvidia tumbled more than 7%, putting the chipmaker on track to shed more than $250 billion in market value and eroding a 31% comeback rally after CEO Huang's reinstatement that added over $900 billion.

The report said current evidence suggests that Alice Huang and Jensen Huang may have had an amorous relationship, but not a coordinated play by China, adding that new information could, however, change that assessment.

The briefing also noted that Kang Wei, described to the Journal as Alice Huang's husband by people who know them, was an asset for China's Ministry of State Security who remained in frequent contact with the intelligence service.

Reporting by Anhata Rooprai in Bengaluru; Editing by Shinjini Ganguli

items.title: US CIA, ODNI suffer cybersecurity breach of some unclassified information, source says
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Nov 24 (Reuters) - The US Central Intelligence Agency and the Office of the Director of National Intelligence recently discovered a cybersecurity breach that exposed some of their unclassified information, according to a person familiar with the matter.

The intrusions affected a network that looks for intelligence insights in public, unclassified material, according to the New York Times, which first reported on the breach.

While it was not clear specifically what unclassified material was compromised, information at other government agencies was also believed to have been exposed in the breach, the Times added.

Asked about the report, the ODNI said there had been "no disruptions to critical capabilities or classified systems."

The news is the latest in a series of tech outages and cybersecurity incidents, including a breach reported at the US Department of Agriculture. Two separate breaches have recently been disclosed at the FBI, while the Pentagon and the Department of Homeland Security have also been caught up in recent cyber incidents.

The Times report did not say how the breach occurred.

items.title: Radar issue delaying flights at Chicago O'Hare airport, FAA says
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Nov 24 (Reuters) - An outage with a ground radar system is delaying flights into Chicago O'Hare International Airport and could force a halt to arriving flights, the US Federal Aviation Administration said on Tuesday.

The FAA said it "is temporarily delaying some flights while technicians work to repair a piece of air traffic equipment."

Air traffic control uses the ground surveillance radar and tracking system, known as ASDE-X, to monitor aircraft and vehicles on airport runways and taxiways. The FAA warned if the airport became congested, it could again temporarily halt arriving flights.

According to flight tracking website FlightAware, about 13%, or 373 flights, have been delayed at the American (AAL.O) and United Airlines (UAL.O) hub on what the FAA says is the busiest day for flights during the Thanksgiving holiday travel period.

The FAA, which earlier on Tuesday had paused most arriving flights into O'Hare, said delays were averaging 47 minutes and the issue could last until 1 a.m. ET (0600 GMT) on Wednesday. The FAA said some flights were being forced to hold for up to 30 minutes in the air before landing.

The FAA and airlines have faced a series of issues since a router outage triggered a nationwide ground stop on November 13 that lasted nearly five hours and led to more than 18,000 cancelled flights and affected more than 1.5 million passengers.

Reporting by David Shepardson and Jasper Ward in Washington, editing by Chris Reese, Rod Nickel and Lincoln Feast.

items.title: US third-quarter GDP growth revised sharply higher
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Nov 25 (Reuters) - The US economy grew faster than initially thought in the third quarter, powered by robust consumer spending and business investment in artificial intelligence.

Gross domestic product increased at a 4.3% annualized rate last quarter, the fastest pace in three years, the Commerce Department's Bureau of Economic Analysis said in its second estimate of third-quarter GDP. The economy was previously estimated to have grown at a 3.4% pace.

Economists polled by Reuters had expected GDP growth would be revised up to a 3.5% pace. The economy grew at a 2.2% rate in the April-June quarter.

The revision reflected upgrades to consumer spending and business investment. Growth in consumer spending, which accounts for more than two-thirds of the economy, was revised up to a 4.2% rate from the previously reported 3.8% pace.

Spending is being mostly driven by higher-income households, whose wealth was boosted by the stock market, before the recent AI-led selloff. Historically low layoffs and moderate hiring are also helping other households to sustain spending, though wage gains have at times lagged inflation. Households are also saving less and dipping into their nest eggs.

Business spending on equipment increased at a 21.8% rate. That was an upgrade from the 20.9% rate of growth estimated last month. Business investment has posted three straight quarters of double-digit growth, but economists warned that the trend could slow as investors scrutinize AI valuations.

Final sales to private domestic purchasers, which exclude inventories, trade and government, accelerated at a 5.8% rate, the fastest since the second quarter of 2021. This measure of domestic demand, closely watched by policymakers, was previously estimated to have surged at a 4.9% rate.

Profits from current production increased at a rate of $206.0 billion last quarter after rising at a pace of $384.0 billion in the April-June quarter.

When measured from the income side, the economy grew at a 4.4% rate last quarter. Gross domestic income increased at a 2.3% pace in the second quarter. The average of GDP and GDI, considered a better measure of economic activity, grew at a 4.4% rate. Gross domestic output grew at a 2.2% rate in the April-June quarter.

Reporting by Lucia Mutikani; Editing by Paul Simao

items.title: Nvidia faces questions from top Senate antitrust Democrat
items.content_html:
Nov 25 (Reuters) - US Senator Cory Booker, a New Jersey Democrat, demanded answers from Nvidia on Wednesday about CEO Jensen Huang's return, according to a letter seen by Reuters, indicating the chipmaker's market power will be a likely focus of antitrust scrutiny by Democrats.

Booker's request adds to congressional scrutiny of Huang's return and Nvidia's business links to China. Booker is the top Democrat on the Senate antitrust subcommittee and likely to lead it when the next Congress begins in January. Tech companies are expected to face scrutiny as part of a larger wave of Democratic investigations.

Booker asked for information about the Trump administration's communications with Nvidia's board leading up to Huang's resignation and reinstatement, including President Donald Trump's assurances that Huang posed no national security threat.

Nvidia must also preserve board records on the decision and details of its independent investigation on the company's compliance with US export controls, he said in the letter to Nvidia Chair Harvey Jones, dated Wednesday.

Nvidia did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Huang resigned as head of one of the world's most valuable companies on November 12 amid reports of extramarital affairs, including one with a woman alleged to have spied for China. Nvidia reinstated Huang on Monday after Trump called for his return.

The incident roiled stock markets, sending technology stocks sliding and then, when Huang was reinstated, pushing Nvidia (NVDA.O) shares up more than 31%. The stock was down 8% in early US trading on Wednesday.

MARKET POWER QUESTIONS

Booker said Trump's involvement in Huang's reinstatement and the resulting stock market surge raise questions about Nvidia's market power and whether the company is "too big to hold accountable."

"The antitrust laws exist to prevent this kind of concentration where a company is so dominant that a mere change in its leadership threatens household savings and the broader economy," Booker wrote.

Lawmakers swiftly criticized Huang's reinstatement and launched probes. Huang is expected to appear before the House intelligence committee in a closed-door session on December 1 and at a public hearing of the Senate banking committee on December 3.

The antitrust subcommittee has jurisdiction to probe Nvidia's "apparent dominance that has led the federal government to treat its leadership as indispensable to the economy," Booker said in the letter.

items.title: US weekly jobless claims fall more than expected
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Nov 25 (Reuters) - The number of Americans filing new claims for unemployment benefits fell more than expected last week, pointing to stable labor market conditions.

Initial claims for state unemployment benefits dropped 13,000 to a seasonally adjusted 189,000 for the week ended November 21, the Labor Department said on Wednesday. Economists polled by Reuters had forecast 200,000 claims for the latest week. The report was published a day early because of Thursday's Thanksgiving holiday. Claims have been running considerably low since mid-July. Economists still view the labor market as being in a "low-hire, low-fire" state of full employment.

The number of people receiving unemployment benefits after an initial week of aid, a proxy for hiring, tumbled 95,000 to a seasonally adjusted 1.697 million during the week ended November 14. The so-called continuing claims covered the period during which the government surveyed households for November's unemployment rate.

The Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago is forecasting the unemployment rate ticking up to 4.16%, which would round up to 4.2% from 4.14% in October. The jobless rate dropped from 4.5% in November last year to 4.1% in October, though part of the decrease has been due to a smaller labor force amid retirements and the Trump administration's immigration crackdown.

The outlook for the labor market received a boost from a Conference Board survey on Tuesday showing the share of consumers saying jobs were "plentiful" soared in November to its highest level since May 2025, while the proportion viewing jobs as "hard to get" was the lowest in just over a year.

A stable labor market likely clears the way for the Federal Reserve to raise interest rates again beyond December's anticipated hike as it tries to bring inflation under control.

Reporting by Lucia Mutikani; Editing by Chizu Nomiyama

items.title: Nidal Hasan asks US judge for stay of execution for Fort Hood murders
items.content_html:
Nov 24 (Reuters) - (This Nov 24 story has been corrected to say military police shot Hasan, not that he shot himself, in paragraph 7.)

Nidal Hasan, the former US Army major sentenced to be executed next week at the same Fort Hood military base where he murdered 13 people in 2009, asked a federal judge on Tuesday to halt the execution while he mounts a legal challenge to his sentence.

President Donald Trump in October approved the firing squad execution of Hasan, calling him "a very bad and evil man," while Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth made the unprecedented promise to livestream Hasan's death at the Texas military base. Trump scrapped Hegseth's broadcast plans after widespread outcry.

Hasan, imprisoned at the Fort Leavenworth military base in Kansas, has asked a federal judge in Topeka to issue a stay of execution, potentially delaying it by months or years.

US District Judge Anthony Mattivi ordered a hearing about the stay scheduled for Wednesday morning.

Under US law, a condemned person can seek legal review of their detention and sentence, known as a habeas corpus petition, once they have been told the date and method of their execution.

A spokesperson for the Department of Defense did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Hasan, a former Army psychiatrist, used a laser-sighted handgun to kill 13 people in a medical facility at the sprawling Fort Hood base before military police ended the attack by shooting him. Hasan was paralyzed from the chest down and later convicted of 13 counts of premeditated murder by a military court-martial jury in 2013.

The US military has not carried out an execution following a court-martial conviction since 1961, and Hasan would become the first person the US military has executed by firing squad since 1945.

Of the four men on the US military's death row, only one besides Hasan has had an execution approved and scheduled by a US president: Ronald Gray was scheduled to be executed in December 2008, but his execution was indefinitely stayed by a judge through the same habeas petition Hasan is using this week.

Hasan, born in the US to Palestinian parents, represented himself at his military trial. The judge did not allow him to pursue his planned defense that the killings were justified because he was defending the Taliban in Afghanistan from the US military.

In his petition, Hasan said he intends to argue that being barred from advancing this defense at his trial was a violation of his constitutional rights to due process, and that Trump and Hegseth violated military rules when setting Hasan's execution date, including by promising to broadcast his death.

The motion for a stay of execution filed by lawyers from the American Civil Liberties Union of Kansas said that Hasan again intends to represent himself in the habeas proceedings, where a judge will decide if his conviction and sentence were constitutional.

"There is no question that the violence committed at Fort Hood caused unimaginable pain and loss," Anna Arceneaux, deputy director of the ACLU's Capital Punishment Project, said in a statement. "But the gravity of that loss does not change the government's obligation to uphold the principles that define our justice system."

Reporting by Jonathan Allen in New York, Phil Stewart and Kanishka Singh in Washington; Editing by Stephen Coates and Cynthia Osterman

items.title: Trump set to add new sweeping tariffs, undeterred by midterms defeat
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Nov 25 (Reuters) - US President Donald Trump is set to reignite global trade tensions with new tariffs on major trading partners, sources said, undeterred in his protectionist push by major losses by his Republican Party in US midterm elections.

The Trump administration's announcement, expected imminently, will address what it has argued is excess industrial capacity in 16 major US trading partners, three people with knowledge of the matter said on Tuesday.

They include China, which is poised to rack up a record trade surplus of well over $1 trillion in 2026, though the tariff level is expected to remain within the range agreed under the current truce between Trump and his counterpart Xi Jinping.

The prospect of new US tariffs was a further factor weighing on global stock markets on Wednesday as a tech-led rally continued to run out of steam, with Nasdaq futures down over 2%.

"It is another reminder that while the legal justification for tariffs keeps changing, US protectionism is becoming increasingly difficult to unwind," ING analysts wrote in a note.

On Wednesday, Beijing reiterated its opposition to "trade wars" and once again dismissed the notion of overcapacity, but stopped short of threatening retaliation.

"The so-called 'overcapacity' is a false issue, and China opposes using it as an excuse for political manipulation," foreign ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun said.

"Both China and the United States should jointly implement the important consensus reached by their heads of state and maintain the stable development of bilateral economic and trade relations," Guo said.

TARIFF WALL

Analysts say, however, higher US trade barriers against China and other economies are the direction of travel, even if the Democratic Party — which won majorities in both houses of Congress earlier this month — tried to curb Trump's tariff impulses.

The tariffs have in part contributed to higher prices on consumer goods in the US, a major source of discontent among voters.

"Without the two-thirds majority needed to override a presidential veto, Democrats' ability to dismantle the tariff wall will remain limited," ING analysts said in a note.

"Either way, we don't think the blue wave will mark a return to free trade. The Biden years already showed that tariffs in strategically important sectors enjoy support across political camps."

The US-China truce runs until January 10, but many expect it to be extended — potentially as early as next month when Trump and Xi are set to meet again at a G20 gathering in Miami — given the major impact a re-escalation of tit-for-tat hikes similar to those seen in 2025 would have on both economies.

The agreement caps Trump's second-term tariffs on Chinese goods at 20%, in addition to duties of about 25% imposed during his first term. The US has already imposed a 12.5% anti-forced labor duty on all Chinese imports, leaving only 7.5% to reach the 20% cap.

The US and China also are working to cut tariffs on $30 billion of non-strategic imports from each side.

TAILORED RATES

One of the people said that the duties would be specifically tailored to each country, with goods from Mexico and Norway unlikely to see any immediate levies.

The White House is expected to honor capped tariff rates that were included in finalized US trade deals with partner countries, this person said. These include duty ceilings of 15% on goods from the EU, Japan and South Korea and 19% for Malaysia.

The US also is expected to honor the 20% cap on Trump's second-term tariffs on goods from China, as long as a trade truce with Beijing is extended. If it expires, the Chinese excess capacity rate would rise to a higher level.

The USTR and the White House did not respond to Reuters queries about the pending announcement.

REPLACEMENT TARIFFS

The trading partners included in the probe are China, India, Japan, South Korea, Mexico, Vietnam, Taiwan, Thailand, Malaysia, Indonesia, Switzerland, Norway, Singapore, Bangladesh and Cambodia, along with the European Union.

USTR launched the excess capacity probe in March, under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, along with a separate investigation into weak or lax enforcement of anti-forced labor laws in 59 countries and the European Union. Together, the duties are meant to rebuild Trump's global "Liberation Day" tariffs that were struck down by the US Supreme Court in February.

The Trump administration has singled out China as the biggest source of excess industrial capacity, which it says is flooding global markets with steel, aluminum, electric vehicles, appliances, solar products and other goods. China says its exports reflect competitive advantages.

The probe is also partly directed at Chinese investment in Southeast Asian countries, including Vietnam, Indonesia and Cambodia, to manufacture goods for the US market and avoid prior US tariffs.

items.title: East Coast storm to bring rain, strong winds on US Thanksgiving
items.content_html:
NEW YORK, Nov 24 (Reuters) - Storms bringing heavy rain and winds up and down the Eastern Seaboard are threatening to delay flights during one of the busiest travel weeks of the year and could ground some of the biggest balloons in the Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade, forecasters said on Tuesday.

Rainfall rates could reach 1 inch (2.5 cm) per hour at times, with wind gusts exceeding 50 mph (80 kph), according to the National Weather Service.

Onshore winds, king tides — the highest high-tide cycles of the year — and this week's full moon could combine to produce moderate to major coastal flooding from Georgia and the Carolinas to Long Island. At least minor coastal flooding is also forecast across coastal New England.

The National Weather Service issued a coastal flood warning for the San Francisco Bay Area through late Thursday afternoon, warning that flooding could reach 2.7 feet (0.8 meter) in some low-lying areas as near-record high tides swell the region's waterways.

Rain is expected to spread across much of the Southeast on Wednesday, potentially disrupting Thanksgiving travel for millions of Americans, before advancing into the Mid-Atlantic and Ohio Valley by Wednesday night. Washington state and coastal Oregon are also forecast to see rain, with snow in the mountains.

In New York City, home to the 100th Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade, conditions are expected to remain dry for the 8:30 a.m. ET (1330 GMT) start. Rain is forecast to develop by late morning or early afternoon and intensify through the evening. City rules require parade balloons to fly at lower elevations or remain grounded if sustained winds exceed 23 mph or gusts top 34 mph.

The Federal Aviation Administration expects the busiest Thanksgiving travel period in 16 years, with more than 417,000 flights scheduled during the nine-day window. Tuesday is forecast to be the busiest day, with 52,000 flights. The agency said in a press release that rain could affect flights across the Southeast, including Atlanta, on Wednesday before moving into the Mid-Atlantic later in the day.

Reporting by Helen Coster; editing by Donna Bryson and Aurora Ellis

items.title: Wisconsin reports third measles-related death this year
items.content_html:
Nov 25 (Reuters) - Wisconsin reported a third measles-related death on Tuesday, as the United States grapples with its worst outbreak of the viral infection in decades.

The latest death involved an adult resident of Lafayette County, the state's health department said. Wisconsin has reported 918 cases and 19 hospitalizations across 24 counties since August.

An HHS spokesperson said the agency was "saddened to hear of a death in Wisconsin" and that the CDC is working with state and local officials through its Epi-Aid emergency response program to curb further spread.

Earlier this month, Wisconsin reported two measles-associated deaths, involving an infant and a child from Grant County.

"This is terrible news for the nation and clear evidence that reduced vaccination rates are enabling measles to get a foothold in communities across the country," said Frederic Bertley, immunologist and CEO of the Center of Science and Industry.

The US is grappling with its largest measles outbreak in more than three decades, a resurgence driven largely by unvaccinated people that this month stripped the country of its hard-fought measles elimination status.

The country has reported 5,838 confirmed measles cases and six associated deaths in 2026, according to data from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.

However, based on publicly reported state figures, the US has recorded at least 14 measles-associated deaths this year, including nine fatalities in Pennsylvania and one each in Virginia and New York state.

A discrepancy between state and federal death tallies arose earlier this year after CDC, under US Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., began using National Center for Health Statistics mortality data instead of state figures.

The agency has said it is working with the Council of State and Territorial Epidemiologists to develop a standardized case definition for measles deaths.
