items.title: Thomas Markle charged in US on second count of possessing child sexual abuse material
items.content_html:
LOS ANGELES, Nov 24 (Reuters) - Thomas Markle, the estranged father of Britain's Duchess of Sussex, Meghan Markle, and father-in-law of Britain's Prince Harry, was indicted on Tuesday in US federal court on two counts of possessing child sexual abuse material.

The indictment doubles the number of federal charges currently lodged in Los Angeles against the 82-year-old Markle in a case that grew out of an investigation initiated last month in the Philippines, where he previously resided.

The elder Markle was originally charged on November 5 in a criminal complaint with a single felony count of possessing child sexual abuse images.

According to an FBI affidavit filed with the complaint, the material in question was found in two Los Angeles storage units and included two explicit photos of Markle posed with a naked underage girl and other images of him with children in various stages of undress.

One of the photos showed a naked girl in a room that appeared to be part of a motel chain in the Philippines, the affidavit said.

Philippine police said last week criminal complaints had been filed against Markle in the country's Cebu province, where he once lived, accusing him of violating local laws against online sexual abuse and exploitation of children.

Markle has denied the allegations, telling the Daily Mail the claims were untrue and describing them as "sick lies."

He was arrested on November 6 at a Florida assisted-living facility where he has been a patient, and is expected to be transferred to California in the coming weeks to be arraigned in US District Court in Los Angeles on the two-count grand jury indictment returned on Tuesday.

Following a court-ordered psychiatric evaluation of Markle, a US magistrate judge in Tampa, Florida, last week ruled that he was mentally competent to stand trial, meaning that he understood the proceedings against him and could assist in his own defense.

Each count of possession of child sexual abuse material, an offense referred to in the US criminal code as possession of child pornography, is punishable by up to 20 years in prison if he is convicted, the US attorney's statement said.

Meghan Markle, an American actor, has been estranged from her father since the run-up to her marriage to King Charles' younger son, Harry, in 2018, when the duchess has said she first became aware of allegations against her father. She has said she was "deeply distressed" over the matter, which led her to cut off contact between her father and her two children, Archie, 7, and Lilibet, 5.

Reporting by Steve Gorman in Los Angeles; Editing by Chris Reese and Lincoln Feast.

items.title: Trump spares turkeys Freedom and Feathers from fowl Thanksgiving fate
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Nov 24 (Reuters) - US President Donald Trump has described the presidential pardon as "extreme powers." On Tuesday, he used it to spare two turkeys from the imminent threat of becoming Thanksgiving dinner.

Trump granted pardons to Freedom and Feathers, the 4-month-old fowl selected for the annual White House ritual.

Raised at Deans Gap Farm in Fort Seybert, West Virginia, the birds spent Monday night at the lavish Willard InterContinental Hotel in Washington before their White House appearance. Trump said next year's turkeys could stay overnight in the new White House state ballroom, where he said he would also hold the pardon ceremony.

Online voters selected Freedom to receive Trump's formal pardon, but both birds will retire to Texas A&M University after their reprieve.

At Tuesday's ceremony on the White House's new South Lawn helipad, Trump gazed at Freedom and noticed his companion was missing.

"Where's Feathers?" he asked.

The second turkey was resting in the White House, officials said. Trump quipped that he'd run off into the bushes.

Moments later, he rested his hand on the bird's fluffy white plumes.

"Freedom," Trump said, "I just want to say, that you and Feathers, as of this moment, have a complete and total pardon."

The tradition dates back more than a century, when poultry farmers sent turkeys to the White House as holiday gifts, forcing presidents and first ladies to coordinate avian logistics to handle the incoming birds — many of which arrived alive. In 1989, President George H.W. Bush formalized a reprieve for the birds, turning the annual turkey presentation into a pardon.

The rising cost of a Thanksgiving dinner could cast a shadow this year on Americans' turkey-centered feasts.

Holiday staples are 6% more expensive this year than 2025, according to the American Farm Bureau Federation. Turkey prices jumped more than 10%, according to the federation, which cited Department of Agriculture data on strong demand, including for exports, and low inventories.

Consumer prices for other Thanksgiving staples and ingredients, such as ham, milk, dinner rolls, sweet potatoes and cranberries, also increased.

Earlier on Tuesday, Trump awarded the Medal of Freedom, the nation's highest civilian honor, to Rudy Giuliani, his one-time personal attorney and New York mayor during the September 11, 2001, attacks on the World Trade Center buildings.

Giuliani himself was once the beneficiary of a Trump reprieve. Trump pardoned Giuliani in 2025 as he faced legal fallout for attempting to overturn the 2020 election results.

items.title: US Army sets out measures to limit lead dust from Iowa explosives blast
items.content_html:
MIDDLETOWN, Iowa, Nov 24 (Reuters) - The US Army said it was working to keep toxic lead dust to a minimum when it detonates nearly 10,000 pounds (4,500 kg) of degraded lead azide in Iowa on Wednesday, as residents sought clearer information about the risks from the blast.

The controlled blast is intended to prevent the aging explosive from detonating on its own. Residents in southeastern Iowa have struggled to keep up with changing information about where a plume of lead dust could travel after the explosion.

At a press conference on Tuesday, officials said the mitigation measures, some put in place in recent days, included a series of earthworks encircling two subsurface concrete bunkers containing the lead azide, as well as a misting apparatus to dampen the surrounding terrain and a system to flood the blast site with special foam designed to capture dust from the blast.

Acting Secretary of the Army Adam Telle said the detonation at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown was scheduled for 9 a.m. (1500 GMT) on Wednesday, when weather conditions were expected to be "ideal to protect public health and safety across the region."

Lead azide is an explosive chemical used to detonate military munitions. The Army brought stockpiles from installations around the country to the Iowa plant in 2009 after moving away from its use. Officials discovered dangerous crystallization during an inspection in March and have since been seeking a safe way to dispose of it.

MULTI-AGENCY RESPONSE

The Army contacted the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives in March seeking guidance on the stockpile, according to ATF Director Rob Cekada.

Some of the lead azide was already more than 60 years old when it was moved to Iowa, he said.

Cekada said falling temperatures make lead azide more sensitive to shock and friction, raising the risk that it could detonate on its own.

"It's not a matter of if, it's a matter of when, and that would not be a great place for us to be in."

The last major disposal of lead azide was an open-air detonation of 7,000 pounds of the chemical in Colorado in 1977, Army Colonel Aaron Teller, a munitions emergency response specialist, said.

Teller said that detonation occurred with "zero mitigation" and that 75% of the lead particulate remained at the incident site.

"We believe we can reduce that last 25% with the mitigation strategy that we have in place," he said.

Lead exposure can cause a range of health problems, particularly in children, in whom it can interfere with cognitive development, according to Patrick O'Shaughnessy, a public health professor at the University of Iowa. Once it settles in the environment, it does not break down, he said.

The Federal Emergency Management Agency said residents within 5 miles (8 km) of the blast may be evacuated, while those within 5 to 20 miles were advised to stay indoors with windows closed to avoid lead dust exposure.

Army projections released on Tuesday showed lead dust could settle on surfaces as far as 40 miles southwest of the blast site, extending through southeastern Iowa into northern Missouri. Airborne particles could travel nearly 100 miles within eight hours, according to the projections.

The Army said it would release updated projection maps hourly beginning six hours before the scheduled explosion and release a final estimate of the affected area afterward.

Officials said information about the problems with the lead azide stockpile had been made public and town halls had been held to inform members of the community closest to the detonation site.

The Army, however, announced the original date of November 20 detonation date only the Sunday before.

RESIDENTS SEEK ANSWERS

Some residents said changing guidance over the timing of the blast and the likely path of the lead plume had left them confused and frustrated.

Jill Holler, 51, took soil samples from her two family farms near Middletown this week so she can compare lead levels after the detonation. She's also worried about her cattle, which have no indoor shelter.

Holler welcomed the additional information released by the US Army on Tuesday but questioned why it had taken so long, noting that the detonation had originally been scheduled for last Friday.

"I'm not opposed if this is the only safe option," said Holler, who organized a protest in Middletown last week. "What I'm saying is that it's been so mishandled that people are confused and don't trust anything they're saying."

Patrick Wall, a beef field specialist with Iowa State University Extension and Outreach, said he had been fielding calls throughout the week from cattle producers seeking advice on how to protect their herds.

Wall said he only became aware of the planned detonation on November 16 and had since put together recommendations for local producers.

"Communication was probably the poorest part of how this was handled," he said.

Reporting by Renee Hickman in Chicago and Joseph Ax in New York; editing by Donna Bryson and Sanjeev Miglani

items.title: Jensen Huang's return to Nvidia fuels Washington fight over China's chip access
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Nov 25 (Reuters) - US President Donald Trump's intervention to save the career of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang may have settled the question of who will run the world's most valuable chipmaker, but it has only intensified Washington's bigger fight over artificial intelligence, chips and China.

On Monday, Nvidia reinstated Jensen Huang as chief executive officer under pressure from Trump, a stunning reversal following his resignation over revelations of extramarital affairs, including with Alice Huang, a former executive at Singapore-based company Megaspeed accused of having ties to Chinese intelligence.

The decision drew applause from Wall Street. But it worried some US officials and infuriated many lawmakers, both Democrats and some of Trump's fellow Republicans, who said Huang's return imperiled US security and called for tighter control of China's access to advanced chips used in artificial intelligence.

"I have warned the administration from the start about Communist China obtaining our most advanced chips through both smuggling and remote access," said Senator Tom Cotton of Arkansas, the Republican chairman of the Senate Intelligence Committee, in a social media post.

"The controversy with Nvidia and Megaspeed is just the tip of the iceberg, and it's not resolved because Jensen Huang has his job back."

Nvidia shares were down more than 7% on Tuesday after leaping on Monday on news of Huang's reinstatement.

His return to the helm of Nvidia has renewed the debate over how the US should compete in the race to dominate artificial intelligence.

On one side are business figures close to Trump, including Jensen Huang, who have helped steer the administration to a more lenient policy. They contend that the best way to keep China from becoming an AI powerhouse is to sell it high-end American semiconductors, weakening Beijing's incentive to learn how to make them itself.

On the other are China hawks in Congress and some parts of the administration, who want to choke off Beijing's access to the advanced chips that power the leading AI models and that only Nvidia and AMD produce.

Huang is due to be interviewed in Congress next week.

Since the news about his relationship with Alice Huang, and midterm elections that signaled voter unhappiness with the AI industry, US policy has become more hawkish. The Commerce Department on Monday added Megaspeed and several other firms to a trade blacklist, barring US companies from selling them chips and other technology.

Experts doubt that the Nvidia CEO's return will alter that course.

"I think it's going to lead to a tightening," said Aaron Friedberg, a professor of politics and international affairs at Princeton University. "There's going to be a lot of pressure from the Congress to tighten the existing restrictions."

Friedberg added: "This intervention by Trump, it's triggering what I think is going to be a much broader reaction, and it's not just going to be about Nvidia and it's not just going to be about China."

'NOT A PROBLEM'

Trump celebrated his victory on Monday, taking credit for the turnaround in a long interview on CNBC and calling Huang a "national treasure."

"The board decided to do what we wanted to do. And one of the things the board wanted to know: Is there a national security problem?" Trump said. "And after a lot of research ... we said, 'No, it's not a problem,'" he said.

Even before this week, Trump's administration had taken a conciliatory approach to China, reversing some restrictions on chip exports imposed under Democratic President Joe Biden.

Trump last December gave the green light to sales of Nvidia's advanced H200 AI chips to China, drawing criticism from both sides of the aisle.

Beyond the argument that allowing China to have Nvidia chips would make its tech industry dependent on US technology, there has been fear that tougher restrictions could prompt retaliation like extending a ban on exports of rare earth minerals used in electronics, AI hardware and military equipment.

Some analysts say China is keenly aware of the dangers of relying on US exports. "They want PRC companies using Huawei chips, not Nvidia chips. The real speed bump in selling chips to China recently has not been export controls, essential as they are to protect sensitive technologies, but that they've been slow to buy," said Michael Schiffer, a senior fellow at the Center for American Progress.

In recent weeks, US authorities have taken a tougher approach, tightening licensing rules for some chip shipments and overseas data centers serving Chinese companies.

ACTION IN CONGRESS

Three bills making their way through Congress would further tighten China's access to semiconductors: the AI Overwatch Act, which would give Congress power over advanced chip exports, the Chip Security Act, which would require businesses to track their chips to combat smuggling, and the Match Act, which would push US allies to restrict chipmaking equipment.

The Match Act in particular would be seen by Beijing as infringing on China's right to develop, a red line set out by Chinese leader Xi Jinping, Paul Triolo, tech policy lead at advisory firm DGA-Albright Stonebridge Group, said.

"These would also be major breaches of the US-China truce, and Beijing will retaliate strongly to all of these measures, creating another dangerous tit-for-tat cycle of escalation that could undermine the truce and significantly worsen bilateral relations," he said.

Even if tightened restrictions on China do not pass before the end of 2026, Democrats will control large majorities in both the House of Representatives and Senate after January 3. With Republican China hawks, they could pass bills with majorities large enough to override Trump's veto.

For their part, China's policymakers are unlikely to sit still.

"Beijing is unlikely to stake everything on Trump's goodwill and the next president," said Lizzi C. Lee, an expert on technology and the Chinese economy at the Asia Society Policy Institute.

"If anything, expect the push for domestic substitution to accelerate after this episode which already exposed the vulnerability of China's AI ambition."

items.title: China's Huawei convicted in sprawling US criminal trial over Iran business
items.content_html:
NEW YORK, Nov 25 (Reuters) - Chinese telecoms equipment maker Huawei was convicted by a jury in New York City on Tuesday in a sprawling US criminal case on charges that it deceived banks about its business in Iran and conspired to steal trade secrets from American companies.

The verdict came in a criminal case that began in 2018, with the US government the following year placing Huawei on a trade blacklist that restricted its access to US technology amid American concerns that Huawei posed national security risks.

The jury in Brooklyn federal court found Huawei guilty on 10 of the 12 criminal counts the company faced, including bank fraud, wire fraud, sanctions violations and conspiring to steal trade secrets. The jury acquitted Huawei of conspiring to obstruct justice and racketeering conspiracy, a charge alleging the company had acted as a criminal enterprise.

China's foreign ministry said on Wednesday that Beijing opposed US efforts to suppress Chinese companies.

"The Chinese government firmly opposes the US suppression and containment of Chinese companies and firmly supports Chinese companies in safeguarding their legitimate rights and interests," ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun told a regular press briefing in Beijing, when asked about the verdict.

The trial lasted more than two months, with prosecutors calling more than 60 witnesses and the defense calling 15. It was not immediately clear what penalties Huawei will face when US District Judge Ann Donnelly sentences it on September 14, 2027.

Reuters reports in 2012 and 2013 helped expose Huawei's activities in Iran and were discussed during the trial.

"After the media started questioning Huawei's operations in Iran, so did Huawei's banks," prosecutor Meredith Arfa told jurors during closing arguments in the case last week.

Brian Heberlig, a lawyer for Huawei, said the company was disappointed by the convictions but said the acquittal on the racketeering conspiracy charge vindicated its "good-faith compliance culture."

"We fully expect to appeal," Heberlig told reporters.

In a statement, US Attorney Joseph Nocella said, "Few crimes are as serious as Huawei's decades-long pattern of endangering US national security, violating the sanctity of US commerce, and impeding the enforcement of US laws."

China's embassy in Washington did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Asked how much the company may have to pay in penalties, Heberlig said it was premature to comment, but the acquittal on the racketeering conspiracy charge could make a significant difference.

Huawei said in a statement it believed the remaining charges lacked legal or factual merit, adding that the five disputes related to trade secrets that prosecutors had cited were civil matters resolved over the past two decades.

The company said no court had previously found it liable for willful intellectual property misappropriation or ordered it to pay damages for trade secret misappropriation.

Experts have said the case did not undermine Huawei's business, as the company diversified and emerged as a key player in China's push for artificial intelligence.

Huawei said it remained focused on maintaining stable business operations and was committed to long-term investment in research and development.

FOUNDER'S DAUGHTER WAS DETAINED

In December 2018, Meng Wanzhou, Huawei's chief financial officer and daughter of its founder, was detained in Canada on a US warrant, prompting a diplomatic crisis involving the United States, China and Canada.

Meng had been secretly indicted on US charges of misleading an HSBC banker about Huawei's business in Iran, so the company could move dollars in and out of Iran in violation of American sanctions.

Meng fought extradition to the US for nearly three years, before entering a deferred prosecution agreement and flying home to China to a hero's welcome. The charges against her were dropped.

Meng did not testify at trial, though an HSBC banker she met with in 2013 did testify.

The 2018 indictment alleged that Huawei misled HSBC (HSBA.L), Standard Chartered (STAN.L) and BNP Paribas (BNPP.PA) about its business dealings in Iran.

Prosecutors added new charges in 2020, including allegations that Huawei conspired to steal trade secrets from US technology companies over two decades.

THE PROSECUTION CASE

During the trial, prosecutors sought to prove that Huawei stole source code from Cisco Systems (CSCO.O) for its routers, stole wireless telecoms company Quintel's antenna technology, and hired a professor to gain access to a circuit board developed by semiconductor company CNEX.

Jurors watched a video that prosecutors said showed a Huawei employee slipping a piece of a T-Mobile (TMUS.O) testing robot into his backpack, and heard about a Huawei engineer sneaking into a Fujitsu booth at a trade show to photograph a device.

Prosecutors gave jurors a statement attached to Meng's deferred prosecution agreement in which she acknowledged making false statements to HSBC about Huawei's operations in Iran.

The defense argued that HSBC and the other banks knew about Huawei's business in Iran and were competing for Huawei's business.

Heberlig accused prosecutors during his closing argument of having "cherry-picked" a handful of disparate incidents to support their claim of a 20-year conspiracy. Heberlig said Huawei succeeded through "hard work, innovation, and investment in research and development."

The company has more than 200,000 employees and operates in about 170 countries.

Additional reporting by Luc Cohen, Jonathan Stempel, and Eduardo Baptista in Beijing; Editing by Jonathan Spicer, Noeleen Walder and Will Dunham

items.title: 'How to Kill a Federal Judge' author sentenced to 6-1/2 years in US prison for threats
items.content_html:
Nov 24 (Reuters) - A Minnesota man was sentenced on Tuesday to 6-1/2 years in prison after his conviction for writing and distributing a 236-page manuscript titled "How to Kill a Federal Judge" that threatened numerous people, including a judge who presided over an earlier, similar case against him.

US District Judge Karen Schreier during a hearing in St. Paul sentenced Robert Phillip Ivers, 73, after a jury in August found him guilty of mailing threatening communications and threatening to murder a federal judge.

Prosecutors had sought a sentence at the high end of the recommended 97- to 121-month range he faced, saying Ivers' conduct was not an isolated incident and that a message needed to be sent after the number of hostile threats and communications targeting federal judges more than tripled over a decade.

"Ivers's sentence should make crystal clear that such threats of violence cannot and will not be normalized," prosecutors in a court filing told Schreier, who sits in South Dakota but was assigned the case after all the federal judges in Minnesota recused themselves.

Ivers' court-appointed attorney did not respond to a request for comment. In court papers, he asked the judge to show Ivers leniency, citing health concerns.

Ivers, who was previously convicted of threatening to kill a federal judge in 2019, was arrested in September 2025 after staff at a library in Wayzata, Minnesota, reported seeing him print copies of his manuscript.

Prosecutors alleged Ivers gave staff a three-page flyer that described his book as a guide "designed to teach extremists on how to plan, train, hunt, stalk and kill anyone including judges, their family members, politicians and more!"

Authorities said they later found 20 spiral-bound copies of the manuscript in his car.

Prosecutors called the document a "manifesto" and said it named multiple individuals and judges. Between January and April 2025, Ivers mailed copies to all nine US Supreme Court justices, three federal appeals judges, a law firm and a university, prosecutors said.

The document included threats to kill Iowa-based US District Judge Robert Pratt, who before his death in January had, due to recusals by Minnesota judges, presided over a 2019 trial in which Ivers was convicted of threatening to kill US District Judge Wilhelmina Wright.

Pratt sentenced Ivers to 18 months in prison. Prosecutors said that Ivers' manuscript threatened Pratt as well as a lawyer who had testified to hearing Ivers threaten to kill Wright.

"Begging for your life won't do you one bit of good judge," Ivers wrote regarding Pratt, prosecutors said.

Prosecutors initially also charged Ivers with threatening to kill a Supreme Court justice but later dropped that charge.

The case is United States v. Ivers, U.S. District Court for the District of Minnesota, No. 25-cr-00347.

For the United States: Bradley Endicott and William Mattessich of the U.S. Attorney's Office for the District of Minnesota

For Ivers: Glenn Bruder of Mitchell, Bruder & Johnson

Reporting by Nate Raymond in Boston

items.title: Salvadoran migrant Kilmar Abrego Garcia to leave US for Spain
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Nov 24 (Reuters) - Salvadoran migrant Kilmar Abrego Garcia, whose wrongful deportation to El Salvador made him one of the symbols of President Donald Trump's immigration crackdown, will leave the US for Spain on Tuesday, according to a person familiar with the matter.

The departure of Abrego Garcia, 31, would bring to a close a legal fight that, at one point, reached the US Supreme Court. US authorities agreed to the voluntary departure as part of a negotiated deal, the Washington Post reported, citing sources.

Lawyers for Abrego Garcia did not immediately respond to requests for comment on Tuesday. Neither did the Justice Department or the Department of Homeland Security.

"The Administration was forced to come to this agreement that respects Kilmar's will and the due process rights guaranteed to him and to all in our nation," US Senator Chris Van Hollen, a Democrat from Maryland, the state where Abrego Garcia lived, said in a post on X on Tuesday.

US authorities sent Abrego Garcia, who entered the US illegally, to a megaprison in El Salvador in March 2025 despite a prior court order barring his return there because of the risk of persecution.

Officials called his removal an "administrative error," but for months said they could not bring him back, thrusting his case into the debate over Trump's immigration crackdown and deportation drive.

After the US Supreme Court ordered the government facilitate Abrego Garcia's return, prosecutors secured a criminal indictment charging him with human smuggling in a case stemming from an earlier incident. The Trump administration then brought Abrego Garcia back to the US in June 2025. It later attempted to deport him to Liberia after a US judge dismissed the human smuggling charge.

Human rights groups say Trump's immigration crackdown has created an unsafe environment, particularly for ethnic minorities, who have raised concerns about racial profiling.

The Trump administration says its actions aim to improve domestic security and are in compliance with the law.

Democrats, who won majorities in both chambers of Congress in the midterm elections earlier this month, say they aim to hold the Trump administration accountable for its immigration policies.

items.title: Democrats aim to reverse Trump's slashes to US food aid, but path unclear
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Nov 24 (Reuters) - Top Democrats in the US Congress have pledged to reverse President Donald Trump's cuts to food aid benefits when they take control of both the Senate and House in January, though their exact path to do so is unclear.

More than 5.5 million people have lost Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program benefits, also known as food stamps, since the July 2025 passage of Trump's tax law, which cut the aid program by $187 billion, or about 17%.

That declining enrollment comes as Americans face rising food costs, driven up in part by the war with Iran and high diesel prices, ahead of Thanksgiving and the winter holiday season. Food banks have reported sustained high demand ahead of the holidays.

Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer of New York said in an email that "Senate Democrats will fight against Trump's cuts to food stamps, his tariffs, his war, and all other policies that are stretching Americans thin."

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, also from New York, has said Democrats should reverse the cuts, but did not respond to a request for comment. Neither Democrat has offered specific legislative strategies they would use to reverse the cuts.

More than 200 Democratic representatives signed a November 18 letter to Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins urging her to repeal a proposed rule that would threaten SNAP benefits for 6.3 million people by curbing automatic SNAP eligibility for households receiving cash aid from a separate welfare program.

Democrats could pass legislation reversing the 2025 tax law's SNAP cuts and overturning any final USDA rule with their sizable incoming majorities in both chambers. But they will still lack the two-thirds majorities needed to override Trump's presidential veto power.

To do that, they would need significant support from Republicans, who overwhelmingly supported Trump's tax law and its cuts to SNAP.

Trump said last week that he plans to veto legislation passed by Democrats, though he signaled openness to discussion of some policies.

LEADERSHIP CHANGES

The House and Senate Agriculture Committees, which draft the farm bill and could put forward legislation to reverse SNAP cuts, will see new leadership next year.

Three members of the House committee — Vice Ranking Member Shontel Brown of Ohio, Don Davis of North Carolina and Jim Costa of California — are jockeying to replace outgoing Ranking Member Angie Craig, a fellow Democrat who is leaving Congress and who has fought Trump's SNAP cuts.

Brown said in an email that the cuts must be reversed and that they burden both Democrat- and Republican-led states.

"We can't rule in or rule out any legislative vehicle at this point because time is of the essence," Brown said.

In the US Senate, Michael Bennet of Colorado and Ohio's Sherrod Brown are vying to replace Amy Klobuchar, who is leaving to become governor of Minnesota, as top Democrat on the Agriculture Committee.

Costa, Davis, Bennet and Senator-elect Sherrod Brown did not respond to requests for comment about how they would approach reversing SNAP cuts.

Trump last week urged Congress to pass the five-year farm bill, which authorizes SNAP and is several years delayed.

Democrats have said the bill must include a two-year delay to the state cost-share provision of Trump's 2025 law, which will foist billions of dollars of spending onto states for SNAP benefits.

The Senate has yet to vote on the bill with 15 days remaining in its session.

items.title: Trump awards Rudy Giuliani the Medal of Freedom
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Nov 24 (Reuters) - President Donald Trump on Tuesday awarded the Medal of Freedom, the country's highest civilian honor, to Rudy Giuliani, the former New York mayor who became a national figure after the September 11, 2001, attacks and later helped Trump try to overturn his 2020 election defeat.

Trump announced he would honor Giuliani, 82, in September 2025 shortly after the former mayor was badly injured in a car accident. Trump at the time called him "the greatest Mayor in the history of New York City, and an equally great American Patriot."

After the 9/11 attacks, Giuliani became one of the most popular figures in US politics. He launched a Republican presidential bid in 2007, and even after it failed, he remained a prominent conservative messenger.

In a statement, White House spokeswoman Olivia Wales called Giuliani "a dedicated public servant whose decisive leadership has left a lasting impact on New York City and our nation."

Trump awarded the medal in a private Oval Office ceremony.

Giuliani in a statement said he was "honored and humbled" by the medal, and credited advice from President Ronald Reagan, under whom he served as associate attorney general and a US Attorney, for guiding his public service.

"I share the credit with all the men and women who worked with me, disagreed with me, and loved me — particularly those who lost their lives in the causes we undertook together," Giuliani said.

His son, former Trump administration official Andrew Giuliani, told reporters outside the White House that the ceremony was a "special" gathering in which Trump and Giuliani reminisced about their long friendship.

Their alliance deepened after Trump lost the 2020 election. Giuliani advanced falsehoods about the result and the integrity of the voting process. He held a press conference at a Philadelphia landscaping business, where he made claims that were widely rebutted, then another at the headquarters of the Republican National Committee where hair dye dribbled down his face.

His false claims came with legal consequences. He was barred from practicing law in New York, where he once served as the US Attorney in the state's southern district, and Washington, and faced criminal charges in Georgia and Arizona for attempting to subvert the 2020 election results.

Two Georgia election workers won a $148 million judgment against Giuliani in December 2023 for defamation. He "fully satisfied" the terms of the judgment in February 2025.

By the end of that year, Trump pardoned him for federal criminal offenses.

With Giuliani's medal, Trump has awarded the Medal of Freedom 27 times between his two terms. He has predominantly reserved the honor -- designated by President John F. Kennedy for "meritorious contribution" to US security or national interests, world peace or cultural endeavors -- for former athletes. Fourteen of Trump's awards have been to retired athletes, some of whom also served in public office.

He has said he plans to award the medal to retired and scandal-plagued Major League Baseball pitcher Roger Clemens and US national hockey team goaltender Connor Hellebuyck.

Trump posthumously awarded the medal to slain conservative activist Charlie Kirk in October 2025.

Reporting by Jacob Bogage; Editing by Colleen Jenkins and Deepa Babington

items.title: Black Southerners say Democrats wrote them off. Their votes may have changed that.
items.content_html:
HATTIESBURG, Mississippi, Nov 24 (Reuters) - The sun rises every day over a memorial to civil rights leader Vernon Dahmer, murdered in 1966 by the Ku Klux Klan for paying poll taxes for fellow Black voters. Then at dusk, it sets on a 1910 Confederate monument, a symbol of racism to some, just yards away in Hattiesburg, Mississippi.

Melanie Sowell has renewed hope the dark legacy that has long hung over this Southern city will eventually lift.

“One day, if we continue this fight, the sun will set on the segregation, the racism and hatred that we live with every day and fight so hard to combat,” said Sowell, 57, chair of the Forrest County Democratic Party in Hattiesburg.

That hope came closer to reality when Scott Colom, a state district attorney, upset incumbent Republican US Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith in this month's midterm elections, becoming the state’s first Black senator since Reconstruction, the period after the Civil War. Colom won Forrest County, which includes Hattiesburg, by 11 percentage points, though President Donald Trump carried it by 18 points in 2024.

As in Hattiesburg, Black voters across the South helped deliver upset victories for Democrats in proportions not seen in generations.

Black political leaders and organizers have argued for years that Democrats could build lasting political power in the region if the party invested in its large Black electorate rather than writing off Republican-dominated states.

Expanded Black voter mobilization efforts offer a potential blueprint for how Democrats can strengthen their position ahead of 2028 US elections, according to interviews with more than 15 grassroots organizers, political strategists and civil rights scholars.

The question now is whether Mississippi, home to the largest share of Black residents of any state, was an anomaly or an example of a broader phenomenon: a reservoir of Black political power and a growing multiracial coalition that Democrats have underestimated.

The will is there, according to interviews with 19 Mississippi voters. Many say there is palpable energy stemming from anger and frustration that voting rights, jobs and identities are under attack.

“We have done so much to try to get power back in the hands of the people,” said Gloria McCray-Watson, 63, an academic counselor at Jackson State University in Jackson, Mississippi. “And I feel like we got sick and tired.”

UNDERINVESTMENT

For decades, many Democratic strategists have centered national plans on a narrow map of battleground states, leaving much of the South with little sustained party infrastructure or campaign investment.

Marc Morial, president of the civil rights nonprofit National Urban League, said the shift occurred after former President Bill Clinton’s 1990s campaigns, which focused on winning Black votes while also appealing to moderate and conservative white voters. Since then, the Democratic Party has made a long-term retreat from grassroots organizing, candidate recruitment and voter registration, Morial said.

Stacey Abrams, former Georgia gubernatorial candidate, and Black-led organizations spent years restarting grassroots work to turn a once reliably Republican state into a swing state. Democrats won two statewide seats in Georgia, including the governor’s race, in which Keisha Lance Bottoms became the first Black woman elected state governor in US history.

“Black-led organizations never stopped investing where our people are,” said Melanie Campbell, president of the National Coalition on Black Civic Participation, a nonprofit that worked with the NAACP’s “All Roads Lead to the South” voter engagement campaign along with 160 other local organizations.

In Alabama, Democratic US Representative Shomari Figures won reelection despite a dramatic redrawing of his district to make it more favorable to Republicans. Trump had carried the new areas by about 14 points in 2024.

Tennessee State Representative Justin Pearson, a Democrat, ran in a Memphis-area district that Republicans also reshaped. They pushed through a new congressional map that split the Memphis-based district into three. He lost by roughly 1.1 points.

“The important lesson to be learned here is that the Democratic Party’s future flows through the South,” Morial said. “Many of us have been saying over the years that the underinvestment meant that you would have low Black voter turnout in presidential and Senate elections.”

The party, including the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee, defended its approach, saying Senate Democrats flipped nine seats in 2026, including seven in states that Trump carried by double digits in 2024. The committee said it remained focused on expanding the map and would “work to flip every seat we can in 2028.”

“In the face of a difficult map and being massively outspent across the country, Senate Democrats made history by flipping 9 Senate seats, including 7 states Donald Trump carried by double digits in 2024,” a DSCC spokesperson said in a statement.

Though Colom won his election, it came down to “affidavit ballots” — those set aside by poll workers from voters they cannot immediately verify and later counted by hand by officials in court. That process would have been unnecessary if the party invested earlier, widening its margin, according to a dozen party insiders and operatives in the state.

Canvassers in Forrest County such as Seija Hunter had to improvise with limited resources. The 39-year-old nursing assistant said she had only Colom’s name.

“When we started out, we didn’t even have any flyers, so we were going to people’s houses and people would ask us, ‘What does he look like?’” she said. “All we had was a sample ballot.”

REPUBLICANS CITE COST OF LIVING FRUSTRATION

High Black voter turnout is not the whole story, said Williamson County, Tennessee, Republican Party Chair Steve Hickey. Republican losses across the South were a culmination of voter frustration over the cost of living and failure of the party to sustain the economic message that helped Trump win a second term in 2024, he said.

NBC News exit polls show the cost of living weighed on Tennessee voters, with 82% calling it a crucial or major factor in their vote for Congress. Still, 51% said Republicans were better able to handle the economy, compared with 36% for Democrats.

Some Republican strategists caution against viewing Democratic gains as permanent. Diante Johnson, president of the Black Conservative Federation, said the Republican Party’s midterm defeat was driven by lower engagement from Make America Great Again supporters, diminished turnout among young men and lack of funding for conservative grassroots organizations.

“This is the first year since 2016 we did not do any door-knocking or grassroots on the ground. Grassroots has to be funded and it wasn’t funded this go around. A campaign is not a campaign without the coalitions,” Johnson said.

The coalition behind Colom extended beyond Black voters, about 97% of whom backed him, according to NBC exit poll data. About 27% of white voters backed Colom, as did about 9% of those who said they voted for Trump in 2024.

Turnout must remain high for Democrats to hold the ground they gained, said Deborah Delgado, 74, the first Black woman elected to Hattiesburg's city council. She worries that Republicans, who hold the governorship and control both chambers of the state legislature, could enact more partisan electoral maps or tighter voting restrictions.

‘ACTIVATED’ BLACK VOTERS

Leaders say much of voters' motivation came from the Trump administration’s own actions. Federal workforce cuts caused a cascade of job losses among Black voters, said CJ Rhodes, pastor of Mt. Helm Baptist Church in Jackson, Mississippi.

Coupled with the administration’s push to eliminate diversity, equity and inclusion programs and the Supreme Court’s decision to weaken the Voting Rights Act, Rhodes said Black voters across the state were “activated.”

Across Mississippi and South Carolina, nonpartisan voter registration group Registration Nation identified thousands of unregistered Black voters and sought to turn them into votes. It said sustained investment will be crucial.

“You can’t let people vote and then go away,” said Andrea Pringle, president of the organization.

items.title: US lawmakers raise alarm at FAA decision to deploy aviation AI tool nationally
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Nov 24 (Reuters) - A group of two dozen House Democrats on Tuesday raised serious concerns about the Federal Aviation Administration decision to deploy a new AI tool to assist air traffic controllers nationwide on November 10, days before a major system failure.

The FAA in September began using a new software-based AI tool system in the Washington area that uses predictive analytics to improve how flights are managed after awarding an $875 million, 12-year contract to Air Space Intelligence.

The Democrats, led by Representative Rick Larsen of Washington, the ranking member of the House Transportation Committee, criticized the "sudden expansion of a largely untested system" and asked the FAA to answer a series of questions by November 30. "We have yet to receive any substantive information proving the system was properly validated before its nationwide expansion," the lawmakers wrote.

The system, dubbed Strategic Management of Airspace, Routes, and Trajectories, or SMART, uses data to analyze airline schedules, weather, airport capacity, airspace conditions and operational constraints to predict traffic flows and identify potential conflicts before they occur.

The letter cited the nearly five-hour November 13 nationwide ground stop that led flights to be canceled for an estimated 1.5 million passengers due to an FAA telecom issue.

"The federal government is dealing with a crisis of confidence," the letter said. "Americans' faith in the aviation system is shaken. The opacity and inconsistency with which the FAA has handled the SMART rollout threatens to further undermine that trust."

The lawmakers want to know the data used by the FAA to validate SMART operations and what redundancies are in place to "ensure reliable ATC operations in the event of issues or outages impacting SMART."

The lawmakers also cited reports that the FAA may have retaliated against employees who raised safety concerns about SMART's rapid deployment.

The FAA declined comment and said it would respond directly to the lawmakers.

US Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy has called the tool essentially "dumb AI" and emphasized controllers remain in charge, not the software.

The system uses over 200 data streams, creates data visualizations, and produces scheduling recommendations for operations experts to consider passing along but does not involve active management of planes in the sky.
